title: China Rare Earth Suppliers Halt Some US Shipments Ahead of Xi Visit; Hormuz Lull Ends as Brent Nears $95
subhead: Chinese rare earth exporters are refusing some US shipments weeks before Xi Jinping visits Washington, while the Strait of Hormuz returns to active hostilities and a refining crunch pushes Brent toward $95. The Russia-China pipeline file also moved as Novak revived the Power of Baikal talks.

sections.heading: China Rare Earth Suppliers Freeze Some US Shipments Ahead of Xi Visit
sections.body:
Some Chinese rare earth suppliers are declining to ship to the US for fear of repercussions from Beijing, three sources told Reuters, keeping access to critical materials a live problem weeks before President Xi Jinping is due in Washington on September 24. A handful of suppliers have refused shipments since early August, when China sanctioned the Responsible Business Alliance (RBA), a US supply-chain monitor, and companies now fear punishment for complying with the RMI due-diligence audit framework linked to it.

The US administration has repeatedly asked China to honor rare earth export-licence commitments made under the Busan agreement over the past year, and the persistence of the issue has put it on the US planning agenda for the Xi visit, a source said. Reuters notes exports of yttrium to the US are still only about half their 2024 levels despite large shipments elsewhere, while prices for materials with military or sensitive applications (yttrium, indium phosphide, tungsten) remain near record highs.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a quiet form of leverage Beijing can calibrate precisely — refusing specific shipments without an embargo — timed ahead of the September 24 summit. It keeps rare earth supply risk live for US automakers and defense firms even as US officials want a smooth visit.

sections.heading: Hormuz Returns to Active Hostilities as Transit Slumps
sections.body:
The month-long lull in US-Iran fighting ended this week, with the US resuming attacks on Iranian targets along the Strait of Hormuz and tensions over the waterway rising again, according to USNI News. Only two commodity vessels transited Hormuz on Thursday, down from nine a day earlier and well below the 10-day average, per Kpler data reported by Reuters. Iran has also targeted Kuwait, and US Vice President JD Vance said Washington will only resume talks with Tehran when it stops shooting at commercial shipping, describing the confrontation as not a 'war' (per The Nation and Energy Connects).

Despite the disruption, ADNOC appears to be continuing to load LNG onto tankers in the Gulf, according to satellite imagery cited by Rigzone. A Firstpost analysis notes that while pre-war Hormuz transit averaged roughly 20 million barrels per day, tanker-tracking data put August average flows between 4 and 10 million bpd, with a 'dark fleet' of transponder-deactivated tankers still moving about 1 million bpd of Iranian exports.
sections.whyItMatters: The return to strikes confirms neither side has an off-ramp that sticks; Vance's condition effectively rules out talks while shipping remains a target. The persistence of dark-fleet traffic shows sanctions and blockade are being eroded by evasion, not stopped.

sections.heading: Record Diesel Prices Push Brent Toward $95
sections.body:
Refined products, not crude, are driving this oil rally. US retail diesel hit a record $5.848 per gallon on a full-day national average (Reuters, Sept 3), while regular gasoline sits at about $4.07, according to GasBuddy. OilPrice.com reports middle distillate cracks are now trading higher than outright crude prices, and ICE Brent is poised to end the week with a 6% weekly gain, trending around $95 per barrel — the steepest weekly advance since mid-July.

Analysts attribute the squeeze to the Iran and Ukraine conflicts constricting supply simultaneously: Hormuz product flows have been disrupted and Russia's refinery capacity is under pressure. Energy analyst Jaime Brito, cited by 247wallst, frames diesel as 'the blood of the economy' whose cost trickles into every good moved by truck or rail. A Reuters poll separately found analysts still forecast oil holding above $80 a barrel in 2026, with weak Chinese demand limiting the upside.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between record diesel and softer gasoline shows the war is hitting supply chains directly — diesel funds freight, agriculture and construction — so the economic bite of this conflict arrives at the consumer register rather than only at the pump.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Freezes Quotas; Aramco Cuts Asia Prices to Post-COVID Low
sections.body:
OPEC+ is likely to hold October quotas steady at 31.01 million barrels per day, pausing the unwinding of the remaining 1.65 million bpd of supply cuts until at least 2027, according to Bloomberg reporting cited by OilPrice.com. The US-Iran war is capping Middle Eastern producers' ability to raise output even as prices rise.

Saudi Aramco kept its October selling price to Asia at a $2 per barrel discount to the Oman/Dubai benchmark — the lowest since June 2020 — defying expectations of an increase even as Dubai backwardation steepened. The low official selling price signals Riyadh prioritizing volumes and market share in Asia over capturing higher spot prices during the disruption.
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ holding quotas while prices climb means the group is choosing restraint over capturing war-driven upside — a posture that keeps spare capacity in reserve and quietly signals it cannot flood a market whose flows are physically disrupted.

sections.heading: Russia Revives Power of Baikal Talks as Output Slips
sections.body:
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Russia and China are discussing the Power of Baikal pipeline — formerly Power of Siberia 2 — for gas supplies to China, and agreed to continue preparing a supply contract, speaking at the Russian-Chinese Intergovernmental Commission on Energy Cooperation at the Eastern Economic Forum (TASS). Novak also said Russia will slightly cut oil output this year, describing the situation as temporary pending refinery maintenance, and that 94% of Russian oil exports now go to 'friendly' nations.

Context from the missile-war front: Russian oil companies failed to fulfil about 60% of gasoline supply contracts on the St Petersburg exchange as Ukraine's drone campaign against refineries bites (per Missile War Monitor). Novak said Moscow will hold exports back until diesel inventories are sufficient, and that a joint Arctic LNG project with China is also being developed.
sections.whyItMatters: Reviving Power of Baikal is Russia's answer to losing European gas markets — a multibillion-dollar pipeline that shifts Moscow's strategic center of gravity toward Beijing. But with output already slipping and refinery losses from drone strikes, Russia is negotiating from a weakened supply position.

sections.heading: US Structures Venezuela Stake to Block Dilution; IAEA Moves on Iran
sections.body:
Washington structured its 35% position in the Venezuelan oil venture as 'penny warrants' in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), the Betancourt-controlled firm holding 100-year rights to 17 oilfields with an estimated 65 billion barrels of reserves, a US official told Reuters. The warrants give the US the right to buy equity at a token price later, protecting its ownership from dilution as NABEP raises capital; the official said Washington still receives dividends before exercising and holds a right of first offer to buy 20% of output at production cost. Energy Secretary Chris Wright separately said Beijing will have no debt claims on revenue from new Venezuelan output despite Caracas owing China roughly $10 billion (per Bloomberg). Italy's Eni is doubling down in Venezuela on hopes of recovering the $2.3 billion Caracas owes it, Reuters reported.

Separately, on the nuclear front, the US, Britain, France and Germany drafted an IAEA Board of Governors resolution that could report Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear program, to be taken up at the board's September meeting (Reuters/AP).
sections.whyItMatters: The warrant structure shows Washington is engineering the Venezuela deal to lock in equity returns and guaranteed crude offtake before the project matures, while the IAEA push layers a multilateral pressure track on top of the military and sanctions campaign against Tehran — with China's $10 billion claim written out of the new production.

bottomLine: Today's energy map is defined by two crosscurrents. In the Gulf, the Hormuz lull has broken — US strikes resumed, transit slumped to two commodity vessels on Thursday, and a record US diesel price of $5.848 per gallon pushed Brent toward $95, with OPEC+ choosing to freeze quotas rather than chase the spike. Against that tightening physical market, Beijing is quietly withholding some rare earth shipments from US buyers ahead of Xi's September 24 visit, turning a strategic-material lever into a pre-summit negotiation tool; Russia, meanwhile, is reviving the Power of Baikal pipeline talks from a position of eroded refinery capacity. The common thread: in every theater — oil flows, rare earths, gas routes — leverage is being adjusted quietly and precisely rather than through grand declarations.
sources: Reuters (rare earth halt; Venezuela warrants; Hormuz transit data; diesel record; Russia Novak; IAEA resolution), OilPrice.com, Bloomberg, USNI News, Rigzone, Energy Connects, GasBuddy, Firstpost, 247wallst, The Nation (Pakistan), TASS, AP News, Free Malaysia Today, Financial Express
